## 1. Suspiria (2018) is one of the best horror movie remakes ever

Some of the sequences unsettled me like you cannot imagine, the last 15 minutes are some of the wildest I’ve ever seen in a horror movie!

Fantastic remake and Tilda Swinton is a scene stealer.

1. The gathering of the witches and that dark magic ritual they were performing at the end...

It was filmed in such a macabre and eerie way that you can almost imagine actual ceremonies like this taking place in underground hidden places across the world.

The movie was one of my favorite portrayals of witches in cinema. And Tilda is as always a masterclass.

I will never get over the cancelled sequel about the life of Mother Markos and how she became a witch in 1200s Scotland.

    - Yeah. But since Suspiria tanked, they never went through with it.

It was gonna be about Mother Markos in the 13th century living as a charlatan woman and deceiving a group of village women until she became a real witch.

“I have this image in my mind… I have this image in my mind of Helena Markos in solitude in the year 1212 in Scotland or in Spain,” Guadagnino told the site. “Wandering through a village and trying to find a way on how she can manipulate the women of the village.”

He added, “I know she was there. I know it was six to seven hundred years before the actual storyline of this film.”

## 3. Onslaught Review

**Score:** 302
**Body:** Did a Labor Day Double Feature of both Buddy and Onslaught two polar opposite films but it was a fun time seeing both! I haven’t done a double feature since the “Barbenheimer” Phenomenon back in the Summer of 2023 so it was fun doing this sort of event again to conclude the Summer Movie season. While I did like Buddy for what it was I did prefer Onslaught much more it was the better film of the two honestly it is an action packed, horror, exploitation revenge film centered on the Übermensch known as “Super Soldiers" of the Aryan Master Race who are test subjects experimented and funded by the U.S. Government with Nazis behind the scenes (See Operation Paperclip). All hell breaks loose as the Fourth Reich tries to be reignited these “Super Soldiers" are some of the worst of the worst accused of war crimes, butchering people, and some who got shot up to fucking hell fighting in combat in the Middle East. 

What transpires is one bad fucking night for Celeste played by Adria Arjona an Army veteran suffering from PTSD and the aftermath of war she is also a struggling single mother going through a custody battle with her daughter but on the bright side she is one fucking bad ass sniper she can shoot like it’s riding a bike. Celeste tries to make things work with her daughter due to being divorced her daughter Daisy played by Blake Kennedy is sweet, innocent, and knowledgeable for her age but thanks to her Dad she never actually refers to Celeste as her Mom rather she refers to her as Ma’am in various scenes throughout the film. However, as the Übermensch wreck havoc brutally murdering anybody in their way both Celeste and Daisy develop a strong relationship dynamic as Mother and Daughter and as the spectators you can genuinely see this and feel compassion and sympathy for them as they endure survival and hell in the process. Both of these actresses absolutely nailed their roles and they worked really well with each other on screen. 

In terms of other characters Cyrus played by Drew Starkey was great too on screen there is definitely more to his character besides being into kinky shit and collaborating with the Nazis trying to cover up the “Super Soldiers” from being made public. Reginald VelJohnson of Die Hard fame was a blast to see in this playing as Josiah a quiet peaceful man but one bad mother fucker he goes above and beyond helping Celeste I loved his character and rooted for him to make it. Eric Wareheim as Kovacks is an officer of the law who loves the sauce and has a cunt of an ex wife taking everything away from him. Kovacks is an asshole but he does have a purpose being the comedic relief character who grows some mucho cojones and puts himself in the crossfire for others which redeems him from being just an alcoholic douche bag living in a trailer park. 

Lastly, the gun play action and gore are the selling points of this film as well! You are there for the characters and the story but man is the weaponry and creative kills disgustingly entertaining and fun to watch! It definitely will make you go WTF and be surprised quite a few times. I love the gore effects, serious top notch effects all around. I loved what Adam Wingard and his team did with this film. 

Adam Wingard may get a lot of flack or hate from some but I have enjoyed his films most of the time than not, especially The Guest, You’re Next, and of course Godzilla vs. Kong and Godzilla x. Kong: The New Empire. The man loves to make movies and God bless him for it! Onslaught gets an A from me. I will definitely want to revisit it again at some point later on and enjoy it a second time. There seems to be a hint of a potential sequel we shall see but if there is I’m down for it! 

Which film do you prefer, Buddy or Onslaught? If you haven’t seen them do a double feature like I did it’s a fun way to conclude the Labor Day Holiday before heading back to the work week!

- Vets used by the government over the last 25 years now stuck in cycles of violence - either at home, which they can never fully return to, or back in action, never leaving the battlefield

Watch and see Wingard's prophetic voice - who lives, who dies, who suffers, who survives... and does anything really get accomplished or change?

## 4. Why Critics are wrong about Salieri's behavior in the Amadeus Director’s Cut

**Score:** 223
**Body:** In the movie Amadeus Salieri is portrayed as a very moral, and believes in god. He treats women with respect (never even touching his crush) and acts politely to everyone. In contrast, Mozart is shown as disrespectful, vulgar, and womenizer

In the director's cut, there is a controversial scene where Salieri asks Mozart's wife, Stanzi, to sleep with him in exchange for helping Mozart get a court job. Many critics dislike this scene, claiming it ruins Salieri's established characterization.

Salieri was deeply frustrated that Mozart slept with the woman Salieri secretly loved, Salieri asking Stanzi to sleep with him calculated move to get revenge on Mozart's past behavior.

Desperate to save Mozart from poor financial situation. Stanzi comes to his house and actually begins to undress. But right at that moment, Salieri orders her to leave. He never actually wanted her body; he wanted to prove a point.

By stopping her, Salieri shows to himself and to her that he has total power and opportunity, yet refuses to do such thing. It allows him to feel morally superior to Mozart. He indirectly tells her, "Mozart is cheap and takes any woman, but I have discipline. Even when given the chance, I will not degrade myself like he does."

It is actually one of the evilest forms of revenge in the film. Salieri uses his moral restraint not out of kindness, but as a weapon to assert his psychological dominance over Mozart.

### Top 8 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. I guess that explains why she's so hostile to him later in the movie. In the standard version, we don't see that.
  - Exactly 💯 (Very important scene imo).
  - In the extended cut they only have two scenes together. 
In the first one, he calls his servant after she undresses.
In the second one, while taking away Mozart's music from him, she says: "I'm sorry we don't have a servant to show you out"

2. I have only seen the director's cut, I didn't know some people didn't like that scene.

Obviously Salieri's character is not meant to be praised. He can't just love Mozart's music, since he's not the one making it, he wants him dead and/or out of a job. 

In the end he cares more about ego than music itself, and he absolutely loves music, so that's pretty pathetic.

If he truly cared about music he'd be grateful and happy of living and working alongside Mozart and get him hired and working constantly.

Mix that with catholic teachings instilled upon him and he sees Mozart person with Mozart talent as some sort of punishment of God towards him, when he's not even really part of the picture. 

He sees "being the vehicle of masterful music" as a blessing, even more so than actually listening and enjoying the music itself, which is human ego nonsense. 

With all that being said, it's not surprising he tried to hurt and sabotage Mozart family, marriage, work, and compared his power/reach to Mozarts to feel better about himself, since it's all about the ego for him. Obviously, since he's a christian and a music lover, this small feat of power over his wife didn't truly satisfy him, it's nothing compared to the bliss of being God's trumpet.
  - Same pinch! Even I only seen the director's cut so far. I didn't tell sallieri is morally superior than Mozart.

 My point is many critics calls this scence as unwanted. But, I feel this scence is very important to understand salieri 's character.
3. Salieri isn't a moral character, he's self righteous. Arguably, everyone in the film is shown to foolish or over enamoured with themselves, Mozart being an exception because he has the talent to deserve it. The moral characters are Mozart's wife and the attendant priest, both witnesses more than anything.

Salieri is shown to be the most pompous of them all, demonstrated by not only his belief in God, but the embellishment of that belief, assuming to know God's will, and cursing it. Salieri is us, the hard working, the frustrated and befuddled. The good and godly stand aside and are equally puzzled by the madness that comes with jealousy and broken dreams.
4. TIL I've only seen the director's cut of one of my favorite films. 

I agree with you, OP, and find it perfectly in line with his character. As protagonist he's by default the character to whom we owe a sympathetic lens, but he all but spells out that he's a petty and jealous man. He sees his dad's death as God's promise that his prayers will be answered and he will become immensely talented so long as he keeps his end of the bargain. That's not the actions of a moral man -- and if it was, it would have been told with shame and guilt. 

He promised God chastity, but that's not why he didn't follow through with having sex with Constanze. He lusted after his muse, and what upset him was not that she'd had sex, but that Mozart got to "have" her. Salieri getting Constanze to bring the music wasn't to steal it, but to prove that he could; having her undress to have sex with him for her husband's benefit was to prove he could take even more from Mozart and possess *her*. 

Sex had nothing to do with it. Degrading her by having his servant come in while she was nude completed the "conquering army rapes and pillages" goal. His disgust wasn't born of shame at lusting over her, but rather at how unfair it felt that Mozart got to do whatever he wanted to her without having to make any pledge of chastity. 

In my opinion, people who dislike the scene feel that way because they don't like it being spelled out even more explicitly that Salieri is *not a good person*. Inability to recognize that being the protagonist =/= being in the right shows a lack of media literacy. It's no different from people who read or watch Lolita and think it's a love story. 
5. He doesn't just order her to leave. He calls in a servant to show her out. While she's standing there naked. He implies she threw herself at him and he's the one who is appalled. The servant was 100% going to spread this around, of course.

This was powerplay. He intentionally humiliated her *and* even worse, put her in a position where servants would gossip about her and her reputation would be damaged. He was also proving to Stanzi and also himself that she isn't as loyal to her husband as she would like to pretend (absolutely poisoned logic of course, when she was only going to sleep with him to help her husband and he put her in this terrible position in the first place).
6. What critics have complained about this scene? The only ones I’ve ever read mention it for the DC are in astonishment it got cut in the first place, as it aids in the final act and character interactions.

## 5. Buddy Review

**Score:** 180
**Body:** Buddy is a Black Comedy Horror film created by Casper Kelly known for the Adult Swim Skit Too Many Cooks it is Kelly’s first directorial debut. The best way to describe this film is if Barney The Purple Dinosaur kidnapped those of us who grew up watching him back in the 1990’s and early 2000’s and made us do everything he told us every single day and if we gave him an attitude he would murder the living shit out of us! 

This film dead ass plays it straight as if it was an episode of Barney for the first 15-20 minutes before it goes on a bat shit killing spree involving our beloved orange unicorn best buddy “Buddy.” It is definitely not for everybody and it is far from a groundbreaking horror film, it's more of a dark morbid comedy poking fun at nostalgia, Millennials born in the 90’s as well as certain Gen Zer’s born in the 2000’s. It is very self aware and dumb popcorn turn your brain off fun. If you’re into films of this caliber full of nonsense and absurdity this is 100% your movie to check out on the big screen! There is plenty of gore, carnage, and intestines to be had! If you love films such as The Evil Dead, Cocaine Bear, Tucker and Dale vs. Evil, Shaun of The Dead, Abigail and a ton of other horror / black comedy films I’m forgetting to include you will not be disappointed with this one. 

To be clear Buddy is not the next Shaun of The Dead or Evil Dead however, if you’re into those cult classics then give Buddy a shot it really is its own film that certain people will like (such as myself I didn’t love it but I thought it was a decent entertaining Labor Day flick) or absolutely hate it and think it’s a piece of garbage. It won’t float everybody’s boat but if you’re into the horror comedy sub genre I think you’re in for a good time. I do not want to spoil anything but there’s definitely more to the story of this film with our group of kids and their pals trapped in this wonderland fever dream like hell hole Cristin Milioti as Grace and Keagan Michael Key as Buddy are the stars in this film along with the supporting cast of kids. 

The twist in this film is predictable and obvious but it is what it is! I wouldn’t immediately buy this on 4K but maybe if it’s streaming one day I’ll revisit it if I really want to. Check it out for yourselves Buddy gets a B from me! I’m going to do a double feature tonight so stay tuned for my review of Onslaught!

# Top 5 posts from r/TrueFilm day

## 1. Films depicting a very specifically realistic form of sexual desire

**Score:** 62
**Body:** Another post got me thinking about this - everyone’s aware that modern films have fewer “sex scenes“ than in the past, but what I’m interested in is where filmmakers depict a very specific sexual appetite realistically.

Sex in films is either gross-out (either for humor reasons or for transgression) or so choreographed and sanitised as to be representive of sex at all, really, but more of a plot device to say “this is a sex scene” or more pornographically “please find this titillating”.

In real life IME sex is rarely clean and sanitised, and sometimes the act of really desiring a partner overrides a particular barrier of ‘disgust’. I’m thinking of moments where sexual desire is so strong that you’ll overlook imperfect or even kind of gross circumstances to make it happen. When films depict that, which is rare, it’s kind of transcendent because it’s universal human experience that’s barely bothered to be out to celluloid. 

One director who does this well is Andrea Arnold -- her film *American Honey* is filled with sexual desire between our protagonist and Shia Labeouf’s uber-trashy character who looks as if he smells. And yet, she films a sex scene at golden hour (the two on a lawn, with Star removing her dirty tampon before the act) that is somehow almost moving in how it captures that desire for consuming another person overriding our very sense. Another film of hers *Fish Tank* has subtler examples of this. 

I do hope my example makes sense; it’s just a part of life we all undergo that few directors are good at capturing and I’m interested in it (not in a creepy way, just as a matter of craft). 

### Top 10 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. *Don't Look Now* is one of the only movies where I've ever seen where I came away with the feeling that I actually just watched two people who are in love be intimate with each other, not just two actors who are being paid and trying to get the scene over with as fast as possible.

It's not well choreographed, it's messy, it's stupidly romantic, kind of cheesy, there's mistakes... But that's exactly how it is in real life. It seems like it was actually there to show us something rather than to just be "titillating," as you put it.
2. Theres a Japanese movie called In the Realm of The Senses that might be what you’re looking for. 

Hopefully this comment meets minimum word requirements because I really hate that aspect of this sub. 
3. I mean, Shortbus feels like the very obvious fit. It contains unstimulated sex but is filmed in a way where sex is just another way to tell a story. There's a lot of different forms of desire across its cast of characters, and it pretty accurately represents the vibes of what sex/kink/queer parties are actually like. 
4. This scene from Punch Drunk Love. The two characters are saying such ridiculous pillow talk, and they realize that it’s silly, but at the same time it’s extremely real and still very full of desire:

## 2. David Lynchs Lost Highway. Gripping, heavy, overwhelming.

**Score:** 48
**Body:** After *Twin Peaks* came to an end with *Fire Walk With Me* (thankfully only for the time being!), several years passed before David Lynch was once again able and willing to bring a new project to life.  
The right idea eventually emerged through a writing collaboration with Barry Gifford (we remember: the author of the literary source material for *Wild at Heart*).  
Lynch and Gifford formed a wonderful artistic partnership here, one that was remarkably free of mutual explanation and yet somehow resulted in a cohesive and coherent screenplay for *Lost Highway*.

A two-part film, part horror, part noir, with a massive shift at its midpoint, and ultimately something greater than the sum of its parts. Pure mystery, quite literally, because you never find yourself waiting for the kind of neatly presented final resolution found in cheap thrillers that try to charm the viewer with some contrived twist. No, here you are allowed to let yourself go, dream up the missing puzzle pieces on your own, and drown in the intoxication of the images.  
The opening time-lapse sequence on the highway immediately had me completely captivated with its hypnotic quality. A sequence that quite literally sucks you straight into the film. And in the wake of that pull, Lynch once again catapults us, true to form, into the most intimate spaces of human beings: the place where everything can and will go wrong, their own four walls, and the house within the house, the upper room of the mind, the most fragile piece of invisibility on this planet. How wonderful that we have art to make it visible.  
Especially in this first part of the film, I felt countless echoes of *Eraserhead*. That threatening and inexplicable atmosphere building within Fred’s (Bill Pullman) and Renee’s (Patricia Arquette) apartment, an apartment that appears almost endlessly labyrinthine and infinitely deep, concealing secrets and danger. The restrained style of acting, which feels unreal and otherworldly; dialogues punctuated by irregular pauses. Bodies moving with an abstract, extremely slow gait and mannered physicality.

This first half creates an atmosphere so incomparable that I can barely think of another film to measure it against. To name comparisons, I would genuinely have to think for quite some time. Unique.  
An atmosphere as thick as butter. Not even a sheet of tracing paper could fit in between. In some of the most tense moments, I actually found myself giggling quite often, partly out of sheer joy at how unbelievably FUCKING GOOD what was being presented actually was, and partly simply to release and mask the tension I was feeling. Without a laugh here and there, I might otherwise have burst.  
Moments such as Fred’s walk into the darkness, the sex scene, and the Mystery Man’s face appearing on Patricia Arquette practically pressed me into the couch and took my breath away. The Mystery Man, too, once again appears as an otherworldly entity, similar to the Lady in the Radiator from *Eraserhead* or the Man from Another Place from *Twin Peaks*. What does he represent in *Lost Highway*? To me, he is definitely a part of Fred’s subconscious, a reflective figure who accompanies Fred throughout his obsession and distrust within the relationship, documents him (the camera!), and confronts him with everything once again. A subconscious, a kind of conscience, one that is skillfully ignored and ultimately reveals itself as the ugly face within, the rotten core of the human being.

Breathe.  
After Fred apparently kills his wife, he ultimately ends up in prison, whose dream logic naturally makes it perfectly clear that there are no other inmates in this prison. A prison solely for him, chains that one places upon oneself. After a brief visual assault, another man wakes up in the cell.  
Pete (Balthazar Getty), who now has his sights set on Alice (once again Patricia Arquette, this time as a blonde femme fatale), will later be dragged back into the abyss by Pete/Fred with the words, “You’ll never have me.” But she loves him, doesn’t she? Or does Fred/Pete perhaps simply want her to have said that so that he can do what he intends to do?  
The tonal mood of the film changes somewhat in its second half. We briefly leave the absolute abyss in which the film began and move back toward the surface, a little closer to the light, a little closer to the beginning of *Blue Velvet*. Yet beneath this more relaxed atmosphere lies danger, a balloon moments away from bursting, a mood that constantly threatens to tip over, like a dance along a knife’s edge. Essential: Kafkaesque noir. Just as fascinating as the first part of the film, merely appealing to different senses. Cerebral and intoxicating.

The film’s circular logic and its ending ultimately reveal this: such an obsession condemns us to repeat all of our mistakes over and over again. Until we burn out and melt away. Escape may be possible in a geographical sense, but we can never flee from our own minds. We take our bad habits with us wherever we go. And if we should ever return, how? In what form? Changed? For what, and for whom? It is incredibly cerebral, intoxicating, and intellectually compelling to think about everything the film contains.

Of course, a few words about the soundtrack are essential as well.  
Not only about Angelo Badalamenti’s score, which is beyond any doubt, but also about Lynch’s incredible sense of style when it comes to selecting songs.  
Whether it’s David Bowie’s “I’m Deranged,” Lou Reed’s “This Magic Moment,” Marilyn Manson’s “Apple of Sodom,” or Rammstein’s “Rammstein, these are songs that not only accompany and underline the narrative perfectly, but simultaneously become one with the sound design, one with the image.

A film, and Lynch as its creator, that perfectly understands and utilizes his medium and the unique possibilities inherent to it, thereby creating something that could not be realized, or, rather conveyed in any other form. The perfect symbiosis of image, sound, and atmosphere.  
Until now, I had only seen the film once. I liked it, with some reservations, but fortunately remembered very little of it.  
That allowed me to approach the work again with a relatively fresh perspective, and during this viewing I remembered exactly what had prevented me from being completely enthusiastic about it back then.  
I loved the atmosphere of the first half just as much then as I do today. So much so that the second half initially felt like a bit of a letdown, and my interest gradually faded. How stupid I was. Pure foolishness!  
This time, however, *Lost Highway* fortunately never let me go, in fact, I found myself wanting to cling to it.  
That, too, is the magic of a focused retrospective, and it makes itself felt here. Nothing is perceived without context, and one sinks into perfect immersion within the world and the evolution of an artist. You grasp it and truly comprehend it. I simply love that.  
*Lost Highway* is many things at once. Gripping. Demanding. A film that leaves you speechless at times and hits the viewer like a truck.  
But above all, it is Lynch in distilled form, stripped down to the essence and brought perfectly to the point.  
A masterpiece.

## 3. Do you recognize your relationships in the way contemporary cinema portrays love?

**Score:** 12
**Body:** I recently watched the 2024 French adaptation of The Count of Monte Cristo, and something about it made me think about how little the representation of relationships has actually changed in mainstream cinema.

The film briefly shows a lesbian relationship — a few seconds acknowledging a sexuality that historical cinema would once simply have erased.

But then we get Haydée and Albert, and the film spends much more of its emotional energy on an extremely traditional romantic structure: they fall in love, their love is forbidden, they suffer because they cannot be together, circumstances separate them, and finally the obstacles disappear and love can fulfil its natural destination: being together as a couple.

It struck me that contemporary cinema has become much better at diversifying who gets to fall in love, without necessarily diversifying what love is supposed to look like.

We change genders, sexual orientations, ethnicities and family backgrounds — which is obviously a good thing — but very often we keep the same romantic architecture underneath.

Two people meet. Their connection is exceptional. They become uniquely important to one another. Separation means suffering. Reunion means fulfilment. Romantic partnership sits at the top of the hierarchy of human relationships.

A queer couple can therefore inhabit a very conventional romantic narrative.

What makes Monte Cristo particularly funny as an example is that Dumas is sometimes messier than the 2024 adaptation.

Edmond and Mercédès cannot simply recover their former love. Too much has happened. The young Edmond she loved no longer exists.

Their relationship remains immensely important without having to continue.

I find that surprisingly modern: someone can have been the love of your life without therefore having to remain your partner for life. A relationship can end without becoming false.

And yet we still see relatively few serious films about other ways of loving.

Where are the couples who deeply love each other but deliberately don't live together?

The former lovers who become something else without their relationship being presented as a failure?

The people for whom friendship is as important as romantic partnership?

Relationships that are profound but temporary?

People who love someone and nevertheless decide not to build their life around them?

Non-monogamous relationships that aren't simply plot devices for jealousy?

Or people who are genuinely happy without organising their lives around a romantic partner at all?

Interestingly, one recent film where I did encounter a genuine critique of romantic fusion was the horror film Obsession. A woman is magically forced to love a man who wants her, and that love becomes increasingly absolute, dependent and invasive.

The clever thing is that the film barely needs to invent the horror.

"I can't live without you."

"I want to be with you all the time."

"You're everything to me."

"I'd do anything for you."

Put swelling music behind those sentences and they belong in a romance.

Push them slightly further and they belong in a horror film.

I found it fascinating — and slightly depressing — that I had to watch a horror film to see romantic fusion seriously questioned.

So I'm curious: do you actually recognize your own relationships, or those around you, in contemporary films?

And more importantly, what films can you think of that portray love or relationships differently?

Not necessarily queer relationships — I'm interested in films that genuinely challenge the structure of the traditional romantic story: separate lives, unconventional couples, friendship, temporary love, non-monogamy, intimacy without couplehood, relationships that change form, or simply love that doesn't need to end in "being together."
